guidance: AD Cu catalysts using carbon-based supports will enhance electron transfer efficiency and stability during eCO2RR.
explanation: Carbon-based materials exhibit excellent stability and high specific surface area, effectively supporting the dispersion of copper atoms and preventing agglomeration. They also demonstrate outstanding electrical conductivity, facilitating efficient electron transport.
methods: Support engineering: use carbon-based supports (carbon cloth/graphene/porous carbon, etc.)

guidance: Copper-based catalysts doped with heteroatoms (N, O, S, B) will enhance electron transfer to key intermediates and product selectivity.
explanation: Doped heteroatoms alter the electronic structure of copper atoms by forming coordinate bonds or providing additional electron orbitals, thereby facilitating electron transfer to key intermediates. Notably, the diverse coordination configurations of nitrogen atoms directly influence the regulation of product selectivity.

guidance: AD Cu catalysts using bimetallic synergy will enhance the reduction of adsorption energy for intermediates and reaction efficiency.
explanation: The introduction of additional transition metal atoms can leverage synergistic effects between metals, reducing the adsorption energy of intermediates. In the Cu-TM-N-C catalytic system, electrons are generally concentrated at the Cu sites, forming the most active regions.
descriptors: Charge distribution (electrons concentrated at Cu sites)

guidance: Copper atoms using ammonia-assisted defect capture will enhance atomic dispersion and active site formation.
explanation: Ammonia molecules, driven by strong Lewis acid-base interactions, pull copper atoms from the surface of copper foam to form volatile Cu(NH₃)_x species. These species are captured by defects in nitrogen-rich carbon carriers, achieving atomic dispersion.

guidance: Cu-based catalysts using dispersed loading will enhance surface activation energy and *CO binding, promoting CO₂ reduction reactivity.
explanation: Dispersing the load increases the energy of Cu surface active sites, thereby promoting the formation of CO intermediates and enhancing the eCO₂RR reaction rate.

guidance: Cu-based catalysts using heteroatom (e.g., N) doping will enhance CO desorption and suppress excessive hydrogenation.
explanation: Nitrogen atom doping modulates the d orbital center of Cu, weakening CO adsorption and enhancing desorption, thereby reducing over-hydrogenation and improving C₂ product selectivity.

guidance: Cu coordination polymers using dual Cu sites with moderate distances will enhance C–C coupling and OCCHO intermediate formation.
explanation: Moderate spacing between adjacent Cu sites promotes the coupling of CHO and CO to form the OCCHO intermediate, lowering the coupling energy barrier and enhancing the selectivity of vinyl products.

guidance: Cu-based catalysts using oxygen vacancies will enhance *CO and *COOH intermediate adsorption and improve C₂ product selectivity.
explanation: Oxygen vacancies can provide additional electrons to stabilize reaction intermediates, thereby enhancing the Faradaic efficiency of ethylene.

guidance: Dual-metal CuNi DACs using synergistic adsorption on Ni and Cu sites will enhance *COOH and *OH stabilization, boosting overall eCO₂RR selectivity.
explanation: The CuNi bimetallic catalyst enhances the stability of key intermediates through synergistic adsorption at Ni and Cu sites, thereby promoting the formation of polycarbonate products.

guidance: Embedding highly exposed Cu–Nx sites into microporous carbon using synergistic Cu–N coordination will enhance eCO₂RR stability and selectivity.
explanation: The highly exposed Cu–Nx sites within the carbon framework provide a stable electronic transport network, maintaining long-term catalytic activity.
methods: Support engineering: embed highly exposed Cu–Nx into microporous carbon
descriptors: Microporous structure and specific surface area

guidance: AD Cu catalysts should not be used with high-temperature reduction methods, as it will reduce atomic dispersion.
explanation: The reduction of copper ions at high temperatures promotes the agglomeration of copper atoms, leading to the formation of polyatomic clusters from dispersed atomic sites and reducing the number of active sites.

guidance: Copper-based atomic catalysts should not be used without proper support materials, as it will reduce stability and catalytic activity.
explanation: Due to the high surface energy of copper atoms, the absence of suitable carriers can lead to atomic migration, lattice substitution, and interface reconstruction, or even the formation of large clusters or nanoparticles. This reduces active sites and causes catalyst deactivation.
descriptors: Tendency for lattice substitution and interface reconstruction

guidance: AD Cu catalysts should not be used with room temperature electrodeposition, as it will reduce uniform coverage of active sites.
explanation: Room-temperature electrodeposition results in the formation of multilayer structures with uneven coverage, affecting the distribution and exposure of catalytic active sites.

guidance: Cu-based catalysts should not be used under conditions generating excessive *H species, as it will reduce C–C coupling probability.
explanation: Excess hydrogen intermediates can lead to overhydrogenation reactions, inhibiting the C–C coupling process and thereby reducing the formation rate of C₂+ products.
methods: Improper reaction conditions leading to excessive *H (not recommended)

guidance: Cu catalysts with overly strong CO binding should not be used, as it will trigger surface ripening and reduce further hydrogenation efficiency.
explanation: Excessive CO adsorption induces Ostwald ripening, causing active sites to migrate or become deactivated, thereby hindering subsequent product formation.
methods: Surface engineering leading to overly strong CO adsorption (not recommended)

guidance: AD Cu materials should not be used without alloy stabilization, as they are prone to oxidation and deactivation in eCO₂RR conditions.
explanation: Active metallic copper readily oxidizes and deactivates, necessitating the introduction of stabilizers (such as Ni or In) to enhance oxygen resistance.

guidance: Copper single atoms using thermal polymerization with controlled temperature conditions can enhance the prevention of Cu atom agglomeration.
explanation: The thermal aggregation method can effectively suppress the aggregation of Cu atoms on the substrate by controlling temperature conditions, atmosphere, and precursors, thereby precisely regulating the generation and distribution of Cu atoms.
conditions: Temperature: controlled (avoid excessive values to suppress aggregation)
Atmosphere: controlled (depending on precursor and target structure)

guidance: AD Cu catalysts using underpotential electrochemical deposition (UPD) at specific potentials can enhance the relative dispersion of deposited Cu atoms.
explanation: Under UPD potential, when Cu atoms interact with the carbon-based substrate, the corresponding active sites cannot interact with other transition metal atoms, thereby effectively ensuring the relative dispersion of deposited Cu atoms.
conditions: Potential: UPD region (below the equilibrium deposition potential of Cu)

guidance: Copper-based catalysts using wet impregnation followed by acid leaching treatment can enhance specific surface area and average pore size.
explanation: The wet impregnation method is simple to operate and yields uniformly distributed copper particles. Nanoparticles adhering to the surface during preparation can be leached out using acid treatment, thereby increasing the specific surface area and average pore size of AD Cu.
conditions: Process sequence: wet impregnation followed by acid leaching
Acid leaching: controlled acid concentration and duration

guidance: Cu-based catalysts using high CO₂ pressure within 1–10 atm can enhance CO₂ solubility and suppress proton/H₂O competitive adsorption.
explanation: Increasing the partial pressure of CO₂ enhances solubility and reduces side reactions (HER), thereby improving the Faradaic efficiency of the reduction reaction.
methods: Reaction condition control: increase CO2 partial pressure

guidance: Cu–N₂ asymmetric coordination using elevated CO₂ pressure (>1 atm) can enhance methane formation and *CO affinity.
explanation: The asymmetric Cu–N coordination environment enhances C≡O adsorption and activation under high-pressure conditions, achieving high methane yield.
descriptors: Effect of coordination environment on pathway selectivity

guidance: Stable nanofiber Cu–Ni catalysts using alkaline electrolyte conditions (pH > 12) can enhance oxidation resistance and maintain FECO > 90%.
explanation: The difference in electronegativity between Cu and Ni in an alkaline environment helps suppress Cu oxidation, thereby enhancing CO selectivity and stability.
